User.objects.filter(email__iexact=email).first() returns the user regardless of is_active; no is_active check in the whole function
RefreshToken.for_user(user) mints refresh+access for the deactivated account — tokens issued but subsequently rejected at authentication time

CHECK_USER_IS_ACTIVE defaults True; DaventProject/settings.py:161-166 SIMPLE_JWT does not override it

TokenRefreshSerializer.validate loads the user and applies USER_AUTHENTICATION_RULE → default_user_authentication_rule (authentication.py:182-184) returns False for inactive → refresh rejected with 'no_active_account'
Sibling customer Google login explicitly re-checks customer.is_active → 403 (parity gap exists but yields no usable session here)
Full read of SocialLoginQuery confirms zero is_active references (grep across AdminApp/domains/users finds only coupon.is_active in serializers)

reason: Refuted by two independent library-level controls in the installed rest_framework_simplejwt: (1) JWTAuthentication.get_user enforces CHECK_USER_IS_ACTIVE=True (default, not overridden) on every request, so the issued access tokens cannot authenticate to any API endpoint; (2) TokenRefreshSerializer.validate applies USER_AUTHENTICATION_RULE, which also rejects inactive users, so the refresh cookie cannot even rotate. The missing explicit is_active check in SocialLoginQuery/_social_session_response is a real parity/UX gap (200 + minted-but-dead tokens + OutstandingToken rows instead of a clean 403, matching the sibling's explicit check), but the claimed security impact — usable sessions for a deactivated principal — is not demonstrated: the deactivated user gains no API access beyond anonymous/public endpoints.

title: No Origin/Referer check on platform session-issuing endpoints -> login CSRF (session donation) on /api/token/ and /api/auth/google/
description: CustomTokenObtainPairView and GoogleAuthView plant the session cookies (davent_refresh httpOnly + davent_csrf) in the response with no validation of the request Origin/Referer and no pre-session anti-CSRF token. DRF APIViews are csrf_exempt (rest_framework/views.py:149), the endpoints accept application/x-www-form-urlencoded bodies (a plain cross-site HTML form POST parses into request.data), and SameSite=Lax does not prevent a top-level navigation POST response from storing Set-Cookie. An attacker auto-submitting a form with THEIR credentials (password, or a Google credential minted with the public client_id from /api/config/) leaves the victim's browser holding the attacker's refresh+CSRF cookies; the SPA's silent refresh then logs the victim into the attacker's account, and everything the victim subsequently enters (billing PII, store content) is visible to the attacker. The buyer-side auth implements exactly this defense — _session_origin_allowed is invoked on register/login/google — but it was never ported to the platform auth views.
root_cause: Missing origin binding on cookie-session issuance: neither CustomTokenObtainPairView.post (auth_views.py:232) nor GoogleAuthView.post/_social_session_response (auth_views.py:435-460,529-538) checks Origin/Referer against the request host or trusted origins, unlike the sibling customer endpoints.
intended_behavior: Session-issuing endpoints must reject cross-site POSTs (Origin/Referer allowlist = request host + CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS + CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS), matching _session_origin_allowed semantics used for customer auth.

post() performs lockout+auth and sets cookies — no Origin/Referer validation anywhere in AdminApp auth (grep for Origin/Referer/Sec-Fetch across the domain returns only unrelated comments)

APIView.as_view returns csrf_exempt(view) — Django CsrfViewMiddleware (settings.py:253) does not apply; JWT auth means no Django session CSRF either

AdminLoginRateLimitMiddleware.guarded_paths covers only the Django admin login/password-reset paths; the other project middlewares add request IDs, headers, canonical host and body caps — no Origin/Referer/session-origin check for /api/token/
